answer: i'm already regretting my decision to move to the countryside
other_correct: i'm regretting my decision to move to the countryside already
wrong_options_that_fit: already i'm regretting my decision to move to the countryside (fronted 'already': marked/literary, but not clearly wrong)
instruction_problem: The end position of 'already' is just as natural in spoken British English, so it has to be accepted. Fronted 'already' is borderline.
level_problem: Probably B1/B2: present continuous with 'regret' + noun + infinitive post-modifier ('decision to move'). No C1 structure. If the target is regret + -ing/to-infinitive, the sentence doesn't test it.

answer: the interview was much harder than i had expected it to be
other_correct: i had expected the interview to be much harder than it was
it was much harder than i had expected the interview to be
instruction_problem: 'i had expected the interview to be much harder than it was' uses every card and is fully natural, but it means the opposite (the interview was easier). With no context, the learner cannot tell which one is meant. 'it was much harder than i had expected the interview to be' is also grammatical; 'it' just needs an antecedent.
level_problem: Comparative + 'than I had expected (it to be)' is B2 (Murphy/Hewings comparatives). Borderline C1 at best.
sense_problem: There are two opposite meanings and no context to choose between them.

answer: i'm afraid i'd have to disagree with you on that
other_correct: i'm afraid i'd have to disagree on that with you
i'd have to disagree with you on that i'm afraid (if a comma before the tag may be left out)
instruction_problem: 'on that with you' is less usual but grammatical. The tag-final 'i'm afraid' would normally need a comma, and comma handling is not specified.
level_problem: This is a functional hedging chunk, closer to B2 than C1, but acceptable.
sense_problem: 'I'd have to disagree' (hypothetical softener) is fine, though 'I have to disagree' is more usual. No real problem.

wrong_options_that_fit: could go: grammatical on the surface, but it is a single specific achievement in a past affirmative, so 'could' is wrong (Murphy: was able to/managed to/was allowed to). 'go onto the plane' is also an odd collocation (get on/board).
instruction_problem: 'could go' fits syntactically, and many learners and even natives might accept it; the distinction depends entirely on the single-occasion rule. This works as a test of that rule, but the key should be explicit.
level_problem: could vs was allowed/was able to for a single past occasion is B1/B2 (Murphy unit on could/was able to). Not really C1.

answer: the committee insisted that the decision be announced to all the staff
other_correct: the committee all insisted that the decision be announced to the staff
all the committee insisted that the decision be announced to the staff
the staff insisted that the decision be announced to all the committee
all the staff insisted that the decision be announced to the committee
the staff all insisted that the decision be announced to the committee
instruction_problem: Serious ambiguity. 'committee' and 'staff' can swap roles, and 'all' can float (all the X / the X all / to all the X). That gives at least 6 grammatical orders, and all are plausible.
level_problem: The mandative subjunctive ('insisted that ... be announced') is suitable for C1.
sense_problem: Several readings are equally plausible, and no context fixes who insisted or who was told.

answer: it's not the kind of job you can walk away from
wrong_options_that_fit: it's the kind of job you can not walk away from: separate 'can not' is a non-standard spelling of 'cannot'. With the stress on 'not' it could even mean 'you can choose not to'. It is marginal, and a lenient checker might accept it.
instruction_problem: The only problem is the marginal 'can not' order, which the checker should decide on explicitly.
level_problem: A contact relative clause with a stranded preposition ('walk away from') is B2. It is fine for C1 but not demanding.
